doc.title: Howie Shear interviewed by Monk Rowe, Dunkirk, New York, October 11, 2014

chapter: Jazz as a career and wrap-up
title: Teaching schedule and returning to Fredonia
summary: Shear explains how he handles subs for his classes and his past visits to Fredonia, including an artist residency.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: So do all your contacts — do they know in Los Angeles that you’re in Fredonia right now?

No. No. And I teach classes at this one school, music theory, orchestration — I told one of my classes, my orchestration classes, that I’m going to be out of town for a week. But I didn’t tell my music theory class. But I did send a sub to teach it. So they don’t have to know. But my orchestration class, they’re a group of composers. It’s a required class. And they need to know how a composer lives his life. My music theory students don’t really need to know that now. If they were in my composition classes I would. And I say okay this is what I’m doing, you want to do this for a living, I don’t need to be here, this wasn’t a required thing for me, but yet I wanted to bring a new chart along that I wrote, and see people that I used to know from a long time ago to see what they’re doing. And it’s networking for me too. In the mid 80s through the late 90s I used to come back here to Fredonia once a year for two, three weeks, and one time I came back for eight weeks as an artist in residence. And it was a great time for me because I got to come to a place I really love to visit. So my composition students know. Because again, I felt like it was very necessary for them to know the things you might have to do as a composer or an orchestrator. So they know.
